question: A training lead asked for a course overview and got four short paragraphs where a detailed document was needed. Which two prompt revisions best address a response that is too brief? Select two.
options: A) Request twice as many overviews so there is more material to choose between later.
B) Ask for the answer as bullet points rather than the paragraphs that were returned.
C) Set out the sections required and what each of them has to cover for this audience.
D) Ask for the same overview again and add the note "please give me much more detail".
E) Say who will read it and why they need the reasoning as well as the conclusions.
correct_answers: C) Set out the sections required and what each of them has to cover for this audience.
E) Say who will read it and why they need the reasoning as well as the conclusions.
explanations: Several shallow overviews are no substitute for one adequate document, and comparing them costs time without raising the depth of any of them.
Bullets change the presentation only. Reformatting thin content tends to make it look even thinner rather than adding what is missing.
Correct. A required section list converts "more detail" into a concrete specification, and it makes any remaining gap visible when the next draft arrives.
"More detail" without a definition of detail is guesswork. It is the standard weak retry and usually returns a slightly longer version of the same thing.
Correct. Audience and purpose set the depth from a different direction: they tell Claude which explanations matter, not merely how many headings to fill.
